1:
The psalm opens on a particle and a noun that no two of them render alike. Spurgeon takes the first word for "only" rather than "truly", since "that faith alone is true which rests on God alone", and gives the Hebrew as "only to God is my soul silence". Clarke refuses the English outright — "I do not think that the original will warrant this translation" — reading instead "Surely to God only is my soul dumb". Ellicott has it "literally, unto God (is) silence my soul", notes that the ancient versions turned it into subjection. Gill keeps both: silent "not as to prayer, but as to murmuring". Henry says the same: the soul "says nothing against what he does, but quietly expects what he will do."

Calvin finds a struggle behind the calm. The word's import is "patient silence", but it is silence achieved: God's people "cannot always reach such a measure of composure as to be wholly exempt from distraction", and here David curbs an impatience already raised in him. Spurgeon makes the silence a work of grace rather than temperament, a bringing down of the will until "we should be wax to the Lord, but adamant to every other force", since "no eloquence in the world is half so full of meaning as the patient silence of a child of God."

On the title they divide over whether Jeduthun received the psalm or gave it a tune. Clarke takes it for the chief of that family's band of singers, men who "prophesied with harps, with psalteries, and with cymbals", and turns aside to demand of their modern successors, "Away with such trumpery and pollution from the worship and Church of Christ!" Calvin doubts the dedication, and suggests the words may instead have opened "some song commonly known at that time". Delitzsch and Clarke agree on Absalom's rebellion as the occasion, Delitzsch pairing the psalm with the thirty-ninth as a twin; Gill keeps both persecutions in view, Saul's courtiers and Absalom.

Augustine reads the title's name as a leaping over, and builds the psalm on the posture that gives: the psalmist stands "in a certain fortified place" from which "he may behold what is below". But the height is the danger, and he is "fearful lest by leaping over he should be proud" — humble not because of what lies below but "because of Him that was above". His answer to the envious is a question: "Shall not my soul be subject to God?"

The architecture of the second verse is what makes the third bite. Ellicott insists that "defence" is "properly, high tower", the metaphor being "important here from the contrast with the tottering wall of next verse"; "shall not be greatly moved" means shall not be made to totter or fall. Clarke measures the same distance: "I may be shaken, but cannot be cast down."

The verb of the third verse occurs only here, and Ellicott lays the renderings out: the Rabbinical "imagine mischief", the Septuagint's "fall upon", the Vulgate's "rush upon" from an Arabic root meaning to storm — which he prefers to "plot against" and "labour in vain". Clarke reaches the same root independently, "to rush violently upon, to assault", and finds the character of the revolt in it — "the disorderly riotous manner in which this rebellion was conducted." Ellicott further prefers the active reading to the passive, giving "How long will ye assault a man? (How long) will ye try to break him down, As if he were a bowing wall, a tottering fence". Wesley hears the appeal as one of kind, made against a man "like yourselves, whom common humanity obliges you to pity". What he is to be cast down from is, for Ellicott, height in that same metaphor; Gill offers the excellency of God, of grace, or of the kingly office.
5:
The psalm turns its opening confession into a command addressed to itself, and the commentators take that repetition as the point. Spurgeon reads it as a guard against relapse: "when we have already practised a virtue, it is yet needful that we bind ourselves to a continuance in it", since the soul "is readily tempted to add a second confidence to the one sole and sure ground of reliance." Gill supplies an occasion: perhaps a new temptation had arisen, "for frames are very changeable things". Clarke turns the waiting into surrender: "resign thyself into his hands; be subject to him, and be silent before him; thou hast what thou hast deserved." Ellicott names what keeps the posture standing: "the state of resignation is one which can only be preserved by prayer."

Spurgeon presses the single eye. The soul is to let none of the enemies' "imaginings, consultings, flatteries, or maledictions" break "the King's peace", but to "conquer by the passive resistance of victorious patience". The reason is arithmetical: "unmingled faith is undismayed. Faith with a single eye sees herself secure, but if her eye be darkened by two confidences, she is blind and useless." Expectation follows the same rule, being "the child of prayer and faith": the worldly man's expectations "promise, but there is no performance", while these "are on the way".

On the seventh verse the point is a preposition. Ellicott gives it "literally, upon God", and Clarke draws out the consequence: "Upon God is my salvation; he has taken it upon himself." Gill reads it the same way, and carries it through to "an everlasting salvation". Clarke alone hears the political register in "my glory", glossing it as "the preservation of my state, and the safety of my kingdom".

Who is addressed in the eighth verse is disputed. Henry opens it as widely as it will go — "You people (that is, all people); all shall be welcome to trust in God" — while noting that the Chaldee restricts it to the house of Israel, who "are especially engaged and invited to trust in God". Gill takes that narrower reading, addressing those "that are Israelites indeed", and defines the trust by everything it excludes: not riches, wisdom, strength, birth or privileges, not the law and the works of it, not their own righteousness nor their own hearts, "but in the Lord only". He adds the Targum's substitution, "in his Word",. Clarke hears something quite different: a loyalist's rallying cry, addressed to "all ye who are faithful to your king", with a prediction attached — "the usurper will soon be cast down, and your rightful sovereign restored to his government."

Henry distinguishes two kinds of trusting and two senses of pouring out. The trust is habitual, "so trust in him at all times as not at any time to put that confidence in ourselves, or in any creature, which is to be put in him only", and also actual, "upon every emergency". The pouring out "seems to allude to the pouring out of the drink-offerings before the Lord", and covers penitent confession; but here he takes it for prayer — "we must lay our grievances before him, offer up our desires to him with all humble freedom, and then entirely refer ourselves to his disposal."

Delitzsch alone reads the section structurally rather than devotionally. Just as all men are perishable with everything earthly they rely on, so "the purely earthly form which the new kingship has assumed carries within itself the germ of ruin"; and God "will decide as Judge, between the dethroned and the usurpers, in accordance with the relationship in which they stand to Him." That is the internal connection of the closing group with the two before it.
9:
The ninth verse sets two Hebrew words for man against each other, and Clarke makes the philology carry the sense: the low are "sons of Adam", the high "sons of substance, or children of substantial men", and a third word yet "properly signifies weak, poor, addicted, wretched man." Neither class can help: common men "are vanity, and it is folly to trust in them; for although they may be willing, yet they have no ability", while the rich "promise much, but perform nothing; they cause you to hope, but mock your expectation."

Spurgeon presses the word that opened the psalm: "here the word is only again; men of low degree are only vanity, nothing more." The multitude "cry 'Hosanna' to day, and 'crucify him' tomorrow"; one may "as well build a house with smoke" as trust "the adulation of the multitude". But the higher class is worse, not better: "we expect something from them, but get nothing." His remedy is the verse's own: "judge them neither by quantity nor by appearance, but by weight." Gill reaches the same distrust from the other end: the wicked poor "are, generally speaking, of all persons, the most wicked; and therefore, though they are the multitude, they are not to be trusted in."

The balance is idiom, and both who handle it say so. Clarke gives the Hebrew as "in the balances they ascend: exactly answerable to our phrase, they kick the beam" — "put both together in one scale, and truth in the opposite, and both will kick the beam." Wesley says it in a line: they are "vain, and helpless creatures" who "generally deceive those who trust in them." Ellicott offers "mere breath" for vanity and agrees, but prefers a small emendation: "a slight change in one letter gives the more probable, when weighed in the scales."

On the tenth verse the readings divide by temperament. Gill takes the oppression either as the power of oppressing or as "riches gotten by oppression"; Clarke hears his own rebellion again, warning the usurpers not to "suppose that my unnatural son and his partisans can succeed", then generalising: "all oppressors come to an untimely end." Ellicott quietly extends the warning past the criminals — "even if by honest means you grow rich, distrust your wealth" — while Wesley keeps it to those feeding themselves "with vain hopes of felicity, from those riches which you take from others by violence".

What "once; twice" means is the real dispute, and Clarke thinks everyone else has got it wrong: "except some of the ancient Versions, almost every version, translation, and commentary has missed the sense and meaning of this verse." His rendering is "Once hath God spoken; these two things have I heard", the two being that God is "the Origin of power" and "the Fountain of mercy" — together "one of the most instructive truths in the Bible". Ellicott takes the numbers as a form rather than a count: "the usual Hebrew mode of emphasising a numerical statement", growing out of a verse structure "which loves a climax." Gill reads the once as finality rather than frequency: God "has spoke often", but "what God has once spoken stands; it is irreversible and immutable." Wesley takes the speaking as repeated, at Sinai and by the prophets, and concludes that power "is God's prerogative; and consequently all creatures, either against or without him, are poor impotent things."

Mercy closes what power opened. Gill takes it as the second thing heard, shown "not only from the common bounties of his providence" but from the gift of the Son. Wesley joins both attributes to the judgment: God being almighty "can easily destroy all his enemies", and being merciful "will pardon good mens failings" — the willingness having been "the only thing that might be doubted, because of their manifold miscarriages".
